title: Now I Am Become Death: New York to Princeton, the fire and the ruin of the atomic prometheus
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Ethical Culture Youth: New York

stops.name: Riverside Drive: the house of paintings
stops.campa: Into a high apartment above the Hudson, Julius Oppenheimer the textile importer and his wife Ella, a painter with a gloved and hidden hand, receive a son. He is Julius Robert, born to money and to pictures: Van Gogh and Cézanne and a Rembrandt hang on the walls, servants move in the rooms, and the great river runs below. The child is delicate, precocious, and lonely, a boy who will collect the mineral kingdom before he learns to fight. The house holds him like a cabinet of wonders. From these rooms the whole arc begins.

stops.name: The Ethical Culture School: Deed before Creed
stops.campa: At seven he enters Felix Adler's school on Central Park West, where God is not spoken but conduct is everything and the motto reads Deed before Creed. Here the non-observant Jewish boy is given a moral universe without a heaven: reason, service, the ethical act as its own altar. He devours English and French, physics, mineralogy. Teachers mark him strange and brilliant. The creed of the deed sinks into him and will never leave; it is the same conscience that later stands, torn, before the bomb. The school forges the moral instrument.
stops.quote_source: Motto of the New York Society for Ethical Culture (Felix Adler)
suggested_refs: New York Society for Ethical Culture Meeting House, 33 Central Park West

stops.name: The New York Mineralogical Club: the boy who read a paper
stops.campa: The child rockhound writes letters to the great mineralogists of the city in a hand so learned that the New York Mineralogical Club invites him to speak, not knowing he is twelve. He stands on a stack of crates to reach the lectern and delivers his paper on the crystalline forms, and the grey-bearded members applaud a schoolboy. Kunz himself presides. The collecting fever, labels, cleavage planes, the geometry hidden in stone, is the first sign of the ordering mind that will later array the elements of the earth toward fission.

stops.name: Joachimsthal: the mines, the dysentery, the delayed start
stops.campa: Graduated from Ethical Culture at seventeen and prizewinning, he is sent by a beloved teacher into the mountains of Bohemia to prospect for minerals: to Joachimsthal, the old silver and pitchblende valley whose ore has just given the Curies their radium and lent its name, thaler, to the dollar. There in the mines he falls gravely ill with dysentery; he comes home wasted, too sick to enter Harvard, and the year is lost to convalescence. The boy who will split the atom sickens, by chance, in the very valley from which the uranium first came. The threads begin to knot.

segments.name: Harvard and Cambridge: The Three-Year Flame and the Poisoned Apple

stops.name: Harvard College: chemistry, and the turn to physics
stops.campa: He arrives in Cambridge, Massachusetts a year late, recovered from the dysentery that felled him in Germany, and falls upon Harvard like a starving man. He majors in chemistry but is seized by Percy Bridgman's thermodynamics; he reads insatiably in six subjects at once, poetry and Sanskrit-adjacent philosophy alongside the sciences, calling himself a 'hot house' of ambition. He is friendless and intense, given to what he names his 'beastly' moods. In three years he takes the degree summa cum laude: the flame burning far ahead of the flesh.
stops.quote: My feeling about myself was always one of extreme discontent.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, recalling his youth (Bird & Sherwin, American Prometheus)

stops.name: Perro Caliente: the ranch in the Sangre de Cristo
stops.campa: Summers he rides the high country of northern New Mexico, and on a rented cabin in the Pecos wilderness of the Sangre de Cristo he shouts 'Hot dog!' And the place is named Perro Caliente. On horseback through the aspen and the thin blue air he finds the two loves that will fuse in his fate: physics and the desert of New Mexico. 'My two great loves are physics and desert country,' he writes; 'it's a pity they can't be combined.' Two decades later he will combine them, on a mesa he can nearly see from here.
stops.quote: My two great loves are physics and desert country. It's a pity they can't be combined.

stops.name: The Cavendish Laboratory: the failure of the hands
stops.campa: At the Cavendish under J. J. Thomson and Rutherford, Oppenheimer discovers a cruel truth: he cannot do experiment. His hands are clumsy at the bench, his soul aches for theory, and the laboratory that is the temple of the atom becomes his torment. He is homesick, jealous, near unravelling; he confesses to friends that he is 'on the point of bumping myself off.' The finest theoretical mind of his generation sits blocking glassware and hating it, and the misery gathers toward a single, poisoned act.
stops.quote: I am having a pretty bad time. The lab work is a terrible bore, and I am so bad at it that it is impossible to feel that I am learning anything.

stops.name: The poisoned apple: left for Patrick Blackett
stops.campa: His tutor is Patrick Blackett, handsome, athletic, everything Oppenheimer is not, who drives him toward the bench he loathes. In a fit of envy and breakdown he laces an apple with chemicals and lays it on Blackett's desk. Blackett never eats it. The deed is discovered; the University moves toward a charge of attempted murder, and only his father's frantic intervention saves him: probation, and a psychiatrist. The genius has tried to kill his teacher with a poisoned fruit. It is the first of his doublings: the maker of death, refusing his own dark hand.

stops.name: Corsica: the island that lifted the darkness
stops.campa: Three analysts fail him; one names dementia praecox and gives him up. Then, on a bicycle tour of Corsica reading Proust by flashlight in a mountain inn, the cloud breaks. Later he calls it not a love affair but love itself: 'a great thing in my life, a great and lasting part of it.' On the maquis-scented island the self-hatred loosens; he chooses to live. The introspective literature does what the doctors could not. He rides down to the boats a man reassembled, and turns toward Germany and the new physics.
stops.quote: Not a mere love affair, not a love affair at all, but love… a great thing in my life, a great and lasting part of it.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, on Corsica (Bird & Sherwin, American Prometheus)
suggested_refs: Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu

segments.name: Göttingen and the Wanderjahre: The New Quantum Mechanics

stops.name: Göttingen: Max Born and the ferment
stops.campa: He comes to the little Saxon town that is, in this hour, the throbbing centre of the quantum revolution. Born teaches, Heisenberg passes through, Dirac and Pauli and Fermi and the young Teller argue in the seminars. Oppenheimer talks too much, seizes the blackboard, dominates until Maria Goeppert circulates a petition to make the American be quiet. But the mind is dazzling now, released from the bench, at home at last in pure theory. In this ferment the shy failed experimentalist becomes a physicist of the first rank.

stops.name: The doctorate: the Born–Oppenheimer approximation
stops.campa: At twenty-three he takes his Ph.D. under Born, and with him publishes the paper that separates the slow heavy nuclei from the fast electrons in a molecule: the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, still taught a century on. His examiner James Franck emerges saying he was glad it was over, for Oppenheimer had begun to ask the questions. The name is now welded into the language of physics. The instrument is finished, tempered, and sharp; it wants only a country and a war to be turned to its terrible use.

stops.name: Leiden: where he becomes 'Opje'
stops.campa: On a fellowship he comes to Leiden, to Paul Ehrenfest, the Socratic gadfly of physics, and astonishes the Dutch by lecturing in a Dutch he has learned in weeks. The students, charmed, give him the affectionate name Opje, which his Berkeley disciples will later anglicize to Oppie, and it clings to him for life. Ehrenfest, wary of his showy brilliance, sends him not to the gentle Bohr but to the fierce Pauli in Zurich, to have the flashiness ground away. The wandering scholar collects tongues and masters as easily as once he collected stones.

stops.name: Zurich: under the lash of Pauli
stops.campa: In Zurich he joins Wolfgang Pauli, the merciless critic whose scorn is the whetstone of a generation, and Oppenheimer, who reveres him, is disciplined at last: his mathematics tightened, his showmanship checked. He works quantum electrodynamics and the physics of the new frontier. But the American in him grows homesick for his own country and its unbuilt physics; a mild tuberculosis is found in his lungs, and the desert calls him back. He turns westward with a European's training and an American's mission, to plant theoretical physics in the raw soil of California.

segments.name: Berkeley: The Charismatic Teacher, the Left, and the Sanskrit

stops.name: Berkeley: the school that gathered around him
stops.campa: He builds American theoretical physics almost from nothing on the Berkeley hills, and a devoted school of students gathers. They copy his walk, his blue shirts, his chain-smoked cigarettes, his way of murmuring 'nim, nim.' He works cosmic rays, neutron stars, and, in 1939, the gravitational collapse that first describes a black hole. Charismatic, cutting, magnetic, he is the professor as sorcerer. Down the hill Ernest Lawrence spins the cyclotron. Here the man becomes a leader of men: the gift that will make him, and unmake him.

stops.name: Pasadena: the migration south each spring
stops.campa: Each spring he descends to Caltech, holding a joint chair, and the whole caravan of his students follows him down the coast: the double kingdom of Berkeley and Pasadena, the two capitals of the new American physics he is founding. Millikan's institute, Tolman, the ferment of relativity and the expanding cosmos surround him. He reads Sanskrit and Dante and French poetry between the equations, cultivating the aesthete's mask over the driving ambition. He is building not a career but a school, a lineage. The men who will fill the mesa a decade hence are being gathered and shaped in these very seminars.

stops.name: Arthur Ryder's study: the Gita in the original
stops.campa: On long winter evenings he climbs to the home of the Sanskritist Arthur Ryder and learns the sacred tongue, until he can read the Bhagavad Gita in the original devanagari: Krishna instructing the reluctant warrior Arjuna to do his duty though it kill. He keeps a worn pink copy on his shelf and gives it to friends. He calls it 'the most beautiful philosophical song existing in any known tongue.' The verses of the field of Kurukshetra, of duty and destruction and the god who is time, enter him now: a seed set twelve years before the false dawn.
stops.quote: The most beautiful philosophical song existing in any known tongue.
sources: Hijiya, 'The Gita of J. Robert Oppenheimer'

stops.name: The left politics: the Spanish cause and the Party's edge
stops.campa: The Depression and the rise of fascism wake him to the world; he gives to the Spanish Republic, marches with the migrant unions, dines with Communists and loves one: Jean Tatlock, who leads him to the Party's fringe. His brother Frank joins; his wife-to-be Kitty is the widow of a man killed at the Ebro. He calls it his awakening to men. He never carries the card, but the fellow-traveling years are sown here, in the cafés and picket lines of the Bay: the associations that a colder decade will exhume to bury him.
suggested_refs: Spanish Civil War Republican fundraising, Berkeley

stops.name: Eagle Hill: Kitty, and the house on the hill
stops.campa: He marries Katherine Puening Harrison: Kitty, a German-born botanist on her fourth husband, widow of the Communist Joe Dallet who fell at the Ebro fighting Franco. Fierce, brilliant, hard-drinking and possessive, she is the storm at his hearth for the rest of his life. They take a house on Eagle Hill above the bay, and their son Peter is born; a daughter, Toni, will follow at Los Alamos. The wandering aesthete is anchored now to a woman as unquiet as himself. The private life gathers its own combustible fuel, to be raked over one day in a Washington hearing room.

segments.name: Los Alamos: The Mesa He Chose

stops.name: Berkeley summer study, 1942: the luminaries and the runaway sum
stops.campa: General Groves, seeking a scientific director, chooses the improbable Oppenheimer: no Nobel, a leftist past, but the one man who grasps the whole. That summer in a locked attic room Oppenheimer gathers Bethe, Teller, Serber and the luminaries to reckon the fission bomb; Teller bursts in insisting the fusion 'Super' might ignite the very atmosphere and burn the world. They compute; the earth is spared. Oppenheimer emerges with the shape of a secret city in his mind, and with the fire's blueprint. The organizer of genius has found his war.

stops.name: The mesa: Los Alamos Ranch School chosen
stops.campa: He rides with Groves onto a piñon-and-pine mesa above the Rio Grande, the site of a boys' ranch school he knows from his own New Mexico summers, ringed by the Jemez and facing the Sangre de Cristo where Perro Caliente lies. Water, isolation, one controllable road, and a horizon of red rock: his two loves, physics and desert country, are combined at last. He chooses this ground. The school is emptied, the barbed wire strung, and a hidden city rises at 7,300 feet to build the thing that ends the war and opens the age.

stops.name: The secret city: six thousand behind the wire
stops.campa: The physicists come with false names to a town that does not appear on any map, all mail to a single post office box in Santa Fe. Fermi, Bohr under the alias Nicholas Baker, Feynman cracking the safes, Bethe heading theory, and over all of them the pork-pie hat and the burning eyes of the director, who somehow holds the moral and the technical and the human threads together. He is the conductor of the greatest concentration of genius ever gathered for a single deed. The mesa becomes the forge of the modern world.

stops.name: Jean Tatlock: the visit and the death
stops.campa: In June he slips down to San Francisco and spends the night with Jean Tatlock, the woman he had loved into the Party years, watched, the whole while, by Army counter-intelligence trailing the director. Six months later she is found dead in her bath, a suicide. The security men note the tryst in their files; it will surface, poisoned, in the hearing to come. The private grief and the machine of suspicion cross here in a single tragic knot. The watchers are already writing the case that will destroy him.
suggested_refs: Army CIC surveillance files on Oppenheimer

stops.name: The Chevalier kitchen: 'the whole thing was a tissue of lies'
stops.campa: His friend Haakon Chevalier tells him at his kitchen, over drinks, that the engineer Eltenton could pass technical information to the Soviets; Oppenheimer answers that this would be treason and lets it drop. But when at last he reports it to security he garbles the tale to shield his friend, inventing three approaches that never happened. Years later, under Robb's lash, he will call the story a fabrication, a 'tissue of lies,' and explain the reason with terrible simplicity: because I was an idiot. The half-truth told in loyalty becomes the noose.

stops.name: Bohr on the mesa: 'is it big enough?'
stops.campa: The old master Niels Bohr arrives under the alias Nicholas Baker, escaped from occupied Denmark, and the mesa reveres him like a prophet. He asks Oppenheimer of the bomb the question that reframes the whole endeavor: is it big enough, big enough not to win a war but to end all war, to force the nations into openness lest they perish? Bohr preaches the open world, the international control that must follow the weapon. Oppenheimer takes the prophecy into himself; it becomes his own postwar gospel, and the seed of the crusade that will make him enemies in high places.
suggested_refs: Bohr's memorandum on the open world

segments.name: Trinity and Hiroshima: The Jornada del Muerto and the Blood on the Hands

stops.name: The Trinity tower: the gadget hoisted
stops.campa: On a hundred-foot steel tower in the desert the plutonium 'gadget' is winched up, its explosive lenses nested around the core like the petals of a lethal flower. Oppenheimer names the test Trinity: from Donne's holy sonnet, 'Batter my heart, three-person'd God.' A dry-run implosion has failed; the physicist Kistiakowsky wagers a month's pay it will work. The rain comes down on the Jornada del Muerto, the Journey of the Dead Man, the old Spanish name for this waterless waste. Through the storm the director waits, gaunt to a hundred and fifteen pounds, chain-smoking toward dawn.
stops.quote_source: John Donne, Holy Sonnet XIV, the source of the name 'Trinity'

stops.name: 5:29:45: the false dawn, and the verse rising in him
stops.campa: At 5:29 in the morning of 16 July the desert turns to a light no man has seen: a sun of a thousand suns, whiter than white, and then the rising fireball and the shock that rolls across the mountains. In the base camp Oppenheimer grips a post to steady himself. Into his mind, he later tells the nation, rises the verse from the Gita: the god Vishnu revealing his world-devouring form to Arjuna. Some laugh, some weep, most are silent. His brother Frank hears him say only: 'It worked.' The age of the fire has begun.
stops.quote: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.
stops.quote_source: Bhagavad Gita 11:32, as recalled by Oppenheimer, NBC 'The Decision to Drop the Bomb,' 1965
sources: Hijiya, 'The Gita of J. Robert Oppenheimer'

stops.name: Ground Zero at dawn: the sand turned to glass
stops.campa: When the light dies the desert floor is fused for hundreds of yards into a green glass, trinitite, where the sand itself was vaporized and rained back molten. The tower is gone, evaporated. Rabi sees on Oppenheimer's face and gait as he steps from the shelter a look he never forgets: 'his walk was like High Noon… this kind of strut. He had done it.' The physicist Bainbridge grips his hand and says the plainer truth. The desert is a mirror now, and something in it looks back. The world is not the same, and they all know it.
stops.quote: Now we are all sons of bitches.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Bainbridge, Trinity test director, to Oppenheimer at Ground Zero
suggested_refs: I. I. Rabi recollection of Trinity

stops.name: Hiroshima: the shadow cast from the mesa
stops.campa: The uranium bomb Little Boy falls over the T-shaped Aioi Bridge and Hiroshima ceases to exist beneath a pillar of fire; some eighty thousand die in the first flash, the shadows of the vanished burned onto stone. Three days later Nagasaki, struck by the plutonium twin the mesa perfected, follows it into ash. At Los Alamos Oppenheimer mounts a stage to cheers, clasping his hands over his head like a prizefighter, and confesses that night he wished only that they had made it in time to use on the Germans. The exultation and the horror are already at war within him.

stops.name: The Oval Office: 'Mr President, I have blood on my hands'
stops.campa: In October he comes to Truman, wracked, and says the words that will ruin their meeting: 'Mr. President, I feel I have blood on my hands.' The President, disgusted, pulls out his handkerchief and offers it: would he like to wipe them? Then he later calls him a cry-baby scientist, snarling that he never wants to see that son of a bitch in his office again. 'The blood is on my hands,' Truman says; 'let me worry about that.' The maker of the fire and the man who ordered its use recoil from one another. The conscience of the deed has come due.
stops.quote: Mr. President, I feel I have blood on my hands.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer to Harry Truman, 25 October 1945 (recounted by Truman and by David Lilienthal)

segments.name: The Postwar Order and the H-Bomb Opposition

stops.name: Washington: the Acheson-Lilienthal plan and the atomic conscience
stops.campa: The most famous scientist in America turns statesman, drafting with Lilienthal and Acheson a plan for international control of the atom: an authority above nations to own the uranium and forbid the bomb, lest the arms race consume the earth. 'The peoples of this world must unite,' he warns, 'or they will perish.' Baruch waters it down; the Soviets refuse; the plan dies. But Oppenheimer becomes the moral voice of the age, chairing the General Advisory Committee, the oracle whom presidents consult. His prestige is a mountain. And mountains draw the lightning.
stops.quote: The peoples of this world must unite, or they will perish.

stops.name: MIT: 'the physicists have known sin'
stops.campa: At MIT he delivers the Arthur D. Little lecture and speaks the sentence that becomes the epitaph of his science: in some crude sense which no vulgarity, no humor, no overstatement can quite extinguish, the physicists have known sin: a knowledge they cannot lose. He does not mean the building of the bomb alone; he means that the pure discipline he loved could logically end in a weapon of genocide, that the tree of knowledge and the tree of death have grown together. The maker of the fire names the wound of his whole guild, aloud, and will not let it heal into forgetting.
stops.quote: In some sort of crude sense which no vulgarity, no humor, no overstatement can quite extinguish, the physicists have known sin; and this is a knowledge which they cannot lose.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, 'Physics in the Contemporary World,' MIT, 25 November 1947
suggested_refs: MIT Arthur D. Little Memorial Lecture, 1947

stops.name: The GAC report: against the Super
stops.campa: After the Soviets test their own bomb, Teller and Lawrence press for the hydrogen Super, a weapon a thousandfold greater. Oppenheimer's General Advisory Committee counsels against it: by its nature it cannot be aimed at a target but only at a people; it is, in effect, a weapon of genocide. 'We believe a super bomb should never be produced,' they write, seeing a chance to limit the totality of war. Truman overrules them and orders the Super built. Oppenheimer has set himself, publicly, against the coming weapon, and against Teller, who will remember.
stops.quote: We believe a super bomb should never be produced. We see a unique opportunity of providing by example some limitations on the totality of war.
stops.quote_source: General Advisory Committee report, 30 October 1949 (Conant addendum, signed by Oppenheimer)
suggested_refs: 1949 GAC report on the hydrogen bomb

segments.name: 1954: The Security Hearing and the Public Ruin

stops.name: Room 2022, Building T-3: the martyr before the Board
stops.campa: In a shabby temporary building beside the Mall the Gray Board convenes, and for four weeks the maker of the bomb is put on trial for his soul. Strauss, whom he had humiliated before Congress, has hunted him; the prosecutor Robb, armed with wiretaps Oppenheimer's own lawyer cannot see, walks him through the loves and lies of twenty years. He sits, gaunt and courteous, a lit cigarette or pipe forever in his hand, watching his life dismantled. The greatest of the physicists is arraigned as a security risk. It is the burning of the atlas: the scientist offered up.
suggested_refs: Gray Board (Gordon Gray, Ward Evans, Thomas Morgan)

stops.name: The cross-examination: 'because I was an idiot'
stops.campa: Robb bores in on the Chevalier story, the cover-tale Oppenheimer once told Boris Pash. Was the elaborate account of three men approached, a lie? Yes. A whole fabrication, a tissue of lies? Right. Why, then, did he tell it? And the most articulate man in America gives the answer that hangs in the record forever: 'Because I was an idiot.' The room is silent. Under the prosecutor's hand the conscience of the atomic age is made to convict himself of falsehood out of his own loyalty to a friend. The deed of shielding has become the instrument of ruin.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, testimony before the Gray Board, April 1954 (AEC hearing transcript)

stops.name: Teller's handshake: 'I would feel more secure'
stops.campa: Edward Teller takes the stand and speaks the words that sever him from the physicists forever: he would feel more secure if the public business were in other hands. He does not call Oppenheimer disloyal, only confusing, and best kept from power. Rising, he crosses to the man he has helped destroy and offers his hand: 'I'm sorry.' Oppenheimer takes it and answers, so the room can hear, that after what Teller has said he does not know what he means. The community of the fire is split in two, and Teller walks out of it, shunned, for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: I would like to see the vital interests of this country in hands which I understand better, and therefore trust more. In this very limited sense I would like to express a feeling that I would feel personally more secure if public matters would rest in other hands.
stops.quote_source: Edward Teller, testimony before the Gray Board, 28 April 1954 (AEC hearing transcript)

stops.name: The clearance stripped: the public ruin
stops.campa: On 27 May the Board rules: loyal, discreet, a genuine service to his country, and yet a security risk, his clearance to be denied. The AEC confirms it on the eve of the expiry of his contract, timing the disgrace for the maximum humiliation. The oracle of the atom is cast out of the temple he built. The nation's most celebrated scientist is branded, in the shadow of Reich and inquisition, a danger to the state. Here the atlas burns: the man of knowledge tried by the fearful state, his fire turned against him. The martyr of the scientists is made.
suggested_refs: AEC decision in the Matter of J. Robert Oppenheimer

segments.name: Princeton: The Institute, Rehabilitation, and the End

stops.name: The Institute for Advanced Study: Olympus of the mind
stops.campa: Even through the ruin he keeps his throne at the Institute for Advanced Study, which he has directed since 1947: the wooded Princeton refuge where Einstein walks the lawns and Gödel paces beside him. He gathers poets and historians among the physicists, presides over Fuld Hall, wrestles with the meaning of what he made. His longest tenure of any director spans two decades. Silenced in Washington, he becomes the philosopher of the atomic condition, lecturing on science and the common understanding, the fire cooled into elegy. The exile keeps his mountain.
suggested_refs: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: The Fermi Award: the rehabilitation
stops.campa: Kennedy chooses to hand him the Fermi Award, the highest honor of the atomic establishment; after the assassination it is Johnson who bestows it in the East Room, before the very government that broke him. Oppenheimer says he thinks it has taken some charity and some courage to make the award today, and the nation reads it as an apology it cannot quite speak. Teller, who won it the year before, is in the room. The state does not restore his clearance; it only lays a medal on the wound. The half-healed prometheus stands rehabilitated, and unforgiven.
stops.quote: I think it is just possible, Mr. President, that it has taken some charity and some courage for you to make this award today.
stops.quote_source: Oppenheimer, accepting the Enrico Fermi Award, 2 December 1963
suggested_refs: Lyndon B. Johnson, East Room ceremony 1963

stops.name: Olden Manor: the throat, the ash, the end
stops.campa: The cigarettes and the pipe take their price: throat cancer hollows the famous voice to a whisper. On 18 February, at eight in the evening, in the director's house on the Institute grounds, the maker of the fire dies at sixty-two. They scatter his ashes in the sea off the Virgin Islands, where he had loved to sail. Hundreds come to Princeton to mourn the man who gave the age its terror and its conscience: Arjuna at the end of the field, the destroyer of worlds who could not put the fire back into the sky. The journey from Riverside Drive closes on a Princeton lawn.
suggested_refs: Olden Manor, Institute for Advanced Study
